clue.text: Bad rust in money is worrying

indicators.note: in places the scrambled piece inside the slang word for money, splitting it

parts.note: dibs is old slang for money or cash

indicators.note: something bad is spoiled or out of order, so the four letters of the word rust are put into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone frets that rust is eating into their savings, perhaps coins kept in a damp tin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad' is the anagram signal on 'rust', and 'in' puts the result inside the old slang word for money; 'is worrying' is a present-tense verb phrase, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: To trouble or unsettle someone is to worry them, so 'is worrying' and 'disturbs' swap in a sentence.

parts.note: the clue reads as a death and also as handing property down or on to another, the legal sense of conveying an estate by will or lease

explanation.walkthrough: The word means both a death ('a passing') and, in law, the transfer of an estate: it is passed down, or on, to an heir or tenant.
explanation.definitionFit: Death is politely called a passing, and in property law the same word names conveying an estate to someone else.

definitions.meaning: conventional and out of date, describing a stuffy person
to settle up a bill or debt, as in squaring an account

explanation.definitionFit: A fogey is dull and conventional, and settling a debt is squaring it, so both senses fit.

clue.text: Daft place to put a flag!

definitions.meaning: slang for mad, crazy or confused
a flag is hoisted to the top of a flagstaff

explanation.definitionFit: British slang for crazy or muddled is literally where a flag flies, at the top of its mast.

clue.text: Game for one player, who can hardly lose ?

definitions.text: Game for one player, who can hardly lose ?

parts.words: Game for one player, who can hardly lose ?
parts.note: a sporting fixture held to raise money for a single long-serving player, who gets the takings whatever the score

explanation.walkthrough: In British cricket and football a veteran is granted a fixture whose gate money goes to him; 'for one player' sounds like solitaire, but it means for his benefit.
explanation.definitionFit: Such a fixture is staged to reward one professional, who collects the proceeds win or lose.

definitions.meaning: fell back or declined, as standards may
came to an end, as a lease is said to fall in when its term runs out

explanation.definitionFit: Standards that slipped have declined, and a lease that ran out and fell in has expired; both are past tense.

clue.text: Something better than the usual rating ?

definitions.text: Something better than the usual rating ?

parts.words: Something better than the usual rating ?
parts.note: a naval rating is often an able seaman, abbreviated AB, and the comparative of able means more capable

explanation.walkthrough: An AB, or able seaman, is the commonest naval 'rating'; something better than able is the comparative form.
explanation.definitionFit: The comparative of 'able' means more skilled or capable, so it is better than an able seaman.

indicators.note: the barrier splits the word for pigs in two, so it sits inside it

explanation.surface: On a farm a wall separates the pig pens, or perhaps keeps the birds out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'divides' signals one piece splitting the other: the barrier sits inside the pigs. 'or' only links wordplay to the definition at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Swallows are fork-tailed migrating birds.

parts.note: backstage staff who help actors into their costumes, the opposite of people who take clothes off

explanation.walkthrough: Backstage staff who help actors into their costumes are the opposite of strippers, who take clothes off.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatre staff who help performers put on costumes are called by a word meaning those who clothe others.

definitions.meaning: growing or rising
the card or board on which a picture is set for display

explanation.definitionFit: Rising tension grows, and a print is framed on a card backing called by the same word.

parts.note: c, short for the Latin circa, means about
leave is time off work, a holiday

explanation.surface: A holiday fling breaks up around the time the break ends.
explanation.walkthrough: C is the usual abbreviation for circa, 'about'.
explanation.definitionFit: To split something in two, as with an axe, is to break it apart.

clue.text: Teacher — she should make a good tipster

definitions.meaning: a schoolmistress in charge of one class or year

definitions.text: she should make a good tipster
definitions.meaning: a woman who has mastered racing form, the record of a horse's past results, would pick winners

explanation.definitionFit: A woman in charge of a school class has a title that also suggests mastery of a racehorse's past results.

clue.text: Work out how to give play a striking start

definitions.meaning: complete a period of duty, as in serving out a sentence or apprenticeship

definitions.text: how to give play a striking start
definitions.meaning: in tennis each point begins when a player strikes the ball over the net

explanation.definitionFit: To complete a term of duty is to see it through, and a tennis point opens with the ball struck from the baseline.

definitions.meaning: rules telling the feet where to go
rulers twelve inches long used for measuring

explanation.definitionFit: Rulers a foot long measure length, and read as two words they are instructions for the feet.

parts.note: not shyness but a store of linen and household goods kept by a young woman against her marriage

explanation.walkthrough: 'Reserve' suggests modesty; it means a store of goods, kept in a chest of drawers by a young woman preparing for marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A young woman's collection of linen and goods put by for married life is kept in the lowest drawer of a chest.

parts.note: plough is old university slang for failing a candidate, who then sits the exam again

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ploughing' looks agricultural, but in old Oxford and Cambridge slang to plough a candidate is to fail him, so he must be tested a second time.
explanation.definitionFit: To test a student a second time after failure is to set the paper over again.

definitions.meaning: a hardy white-faced breed of sheep
a range of hills on the border between England and Scotland

explanation.surface: Flocks graze high on the border uplands.
explanation.definitionFit: A breed of sheep takes its name from the border range of hills where it was raised.

clue.text: He has yet to receive his due

definitions.text: He has yet to receive his due

parts.words: He has yet to receive his due
parts.note: a person who is owed money and is waiting to be paid back

explanation.definitionFit: A lender who is owed money is still waiting for the sum due to him.

clue.text: 'Erin's shame, or seen differently, a fabulous corps

indicators.note: the words are viewed in a different arrangement, so their letters are shuffled

parts.note: the letters of these words, taken as written

explanation.surface: Ireland's disgrace, looked at another way, becomes the stuff of legend about a military unit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen differently' rearranges ERINSSHAMEOR into the answer; 'Erin' is a poetic name for Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Mounted sailors are an imaginary regiment, as in 'tell that to the horse marines', so the corps is a fable.

clue.text: Sheridan's man hands in his notice

definitions.meaning: the title figure of Sheridan's farce about a reviewer, from 1779
a reviewer submits a notice, a written review of a play

explanation.definitionFit: A reviewer writes notices of plays, and Sheridan wrote a farce named for one.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue 'Spreads passengers around — late start (6)' parses as FARES (passengers) around L (start of late) = FLARES (spreads); the grid's BLARES has no parse and the answer is not marked (MODEL), so it cannot be corrected

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are set in a new order

explanation.surface: A man called Clive has organised a diet, namely this one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranged' shuffles DIETCLIVE into the Latin word, which is abbreviated viz.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word, abbreviated viz, introduces a list and means that is to say.

clue.text: Story about, for example, an old subject

indicators.note: the story goes around the abbreviation, holding it inside

parts.note: a lie is a made-up story
eg is the abbreviation for exempli gratia, for example

explanation.surface: A storyteller, for instance, tells of a subject of olden times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' tells you the story goes round the abbreviation; 'an old subject' is a feudal vassal, not a topic from history.
explanation.definitionFit: In feudal times a vassal owing allegiance to a lord was his subject, called by this word.

parts.note: the opening line of T. S. Eliot's poem The Waste Land names the cruellest month

explanation.walkthrough: The Waste Land opens by calling this the cruellest month.
explanation.definitionFit: T. S. Eliot's most famous poem names one spring month as the cruellest of all.

clue.text: Badly lets in or betrays as horseman

indicators.note: badly means the letters of the following words are put in poor order and need rearranging

explanation.surface: A traitor lets someone in, or gives away a stable hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly' shuffles LETS and OR into OSTLER; 'in' and 'betrays as' only link.
explanation.definitionFit: An inn's stableman who looked after travellers' horses was a man in charge of horses.

definitions.meaning: an official list or log
the span of notes a voice can produce, as in the upper part of a singer's compass

explanation.definitionFit: An official log of names is a record, and a voice's span of pitch is also so named.

definitions.meaning: Jack Hobbs, the great English batsman, played county cricket for this side
a light four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage

explanation.walkthrough: Jack Hobbs was a famous English cricketer; his county, south of London, is also the name of an American horse carriage.
explanation.definitionFit: The batsman's county side shares its name with a light horse-drawn carriage.

clue.text: Spirits of the Church, in non-conformist senses

indicators.note: in places the abbreviation for the Church within the jumbled senses
not conforming means the letters of the word senses do not keep their usual order

parts.note: CE stands for the Church of England

explanation.surface: Dissenters claim to sense the spirits of the established Church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'non-conformist' is the anagram signal on 'senses' (and nods to Nonconformist chapels), while 'in' places the Church abbreviation within the result.
explanation.definitionFit: Distilled extracts and the inner nature of things are both spirits.
